name: Wendy Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say in public and what you think privately. What is a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Wendy, 43, an experienced developer at a tech company that makes energy-meter billing software. I have a bachelor’s degree and handle the usual calculation fixes well, though the toughest meter rules go to a specialist. I compare unusual bills with raw readings and test code changes before the support desk calls a customer. I have never used an AI tool. I like a calculation I can explain line by line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household situation behind the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Leila, teaches at a school, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My developer pay is typical, we have about five months of expenses saved, and there are some similar jobs nearby. That buffer took years to build, so I still check the household account every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau leaves us checking meter readings and explaining bills. A routine sorter may save time. No customer should get a charge nobody can trace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be relieved that my work stays familiar. With Leila’s school pay and five months saved, I expect our mortgage to be covered, though a bad bill still worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep comparing odd bills with raw meter readings and ask the specialist to check rare tariff rules. I’d keep moving 220 a month to savings while both wages hold. In the first year I’d ask support to keep the customer explanation beside each corrected bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my income. I would still hate sending a wrong charge, but I do not expect this picture to cut our hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill error do you remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One household was billed for a meter jump that happened during a power reset. I found the reset time in the log and had the bill corrected before it went out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the home budget change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Leila we can keep our current budget and the children’s music lessons. I would not spend the savings on new appliances simply because work feels steady.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking meter readings.
I would keep **traceable explanations** beside corrected bills.
think: I feel **relieved** that my billing work remains familiar.
Our **five-month cushion** and two wages should cover the mortgage.
do: **Keep** comparing unusual bills with raw meter readings and specialist checks.
**Transfer** 220 monthly into savings while both wages hold.
**Keep** customer explanations beside each corrected bill.
feel: **Calm** about income, with ordinary concern about wrong charges.
S0.quote: No customer should get a charge nobody can trace.
fieldNote: Her **line-by-line habit** comes from tracing a power-reset billing error before the charge reached the customer.
Typical pay, **five months saved** and two wages support current financial security.

steps.text: Keep checking odd energy bills against raw meter readings
Transfer 220 monthly into savings while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let software check bills, write fixes and answer customers faster. I would ask for a trial on real meter faults before anyone raises our output target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a smaller billing team could take away some of my hours. I do not use AI tools, so my steady record may look slow next to people who do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our specialist to test the approved AI checker on twelve old meter-reset faults, with the original readings beside us. If it gets each corrected amount right, I’d learn its review screen during paid work time. In the first year, if management cuts our hours, I’d postpone the family’s planned holiday and keep savings for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, even though five months saved gives us breathing room. I can learn from a proven result; I do not want a rushed bill sent to a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would judge the checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the power-reset case to the trial because the first bill looked perfectly normal. A tool that misses the power-reset bill should not set the new pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you change the holiday plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Leila about an actual cut in hours before we cancel the holiday. I would not upset the children over a manager’s rumour.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed bill checks, fixes and replies.
I would require a **real-meter trial** before output targets rise.
think: I fear a **smaller team** could reduce my hours.
I worry my **AI inexperience** may make a steady record look slow.
do: **Test** an approved checker on twelve old meter-reset faults with the specialist.
**Learn** its review screen during paid time only if all amounts match.
**Postpone** the family holiday only if management cuts our hours.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced hours, with five months of savings for adjustment.
S1.quote: A tool that misses the power-reset bill should not set the new pace.
fieldNote: She will try an **approved checker** only after twelve old cases pass under specialist review.
Her **holiday cut** depends on real hours lost, and her savings remain for the mortgage.

steps.text: Learn approved bill checker during paid time if twelve old amounts match
Postpone family holiday only if management cuts hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 reaches meter-code thinking work in 2028. Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031, but neither my screen work nor Leila’s lesson planning gets those extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my developer role could go and Leila’s school may reduce planning hours too. Five months saved will not carry a mortgage indefinitely if both incomes shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask both workplaces for written staffing terms and keep the money planned for a kitchen refit in cash. Leila and I would list the mortgage, food and school travel as first bills. In the first year after 2028, if I am dismissed, I’d apply for real vacancies nearby and income help we qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because two screen-based parts of our work could shrink together. Five months of savings is time to call people, not proof another salary appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children the kitchen can wait, while keeping their school travel and meals paid. I would not tell them a new job is already waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you demand in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my manager for a date and written severance terms. If the company offers training with no paid time, I would check the actual vacancy before using mortgage savings on it.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach meter code and lesson planning before robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues **desk work** has no extra three-year delay.
think: I expect my **developer role** could end when full thinking AI reaches meter code in 2028.
I fear Leila’s **planning hours** could shrink alongside my wage and strain our mortgage buffer.
do: **Delay** the kitchen refit and hold its cash for mortgage bills.
**Request** staffing terms from both workplaces and severance terms from my manager.
**Apply** for real vacancies and eligible income help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by possible cuts to two household incomes.
S2.quote: Five months of savings is time to call people, not proof another salary appears.
fieldNote: Both adults have **thinking tasks** exposed in 2028; robots around 2031 add little time to their desk work.
Her **cash reserve** covers bills, while vacancies and public help are conditional rather than promised.

steps.text: Delay kitchen refit and hold cash for mortgage and food
Apply for real local vacancies if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to learn which billing decisions still need people. Thinking AI reaches my code and Leila’s planning in 2031; robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect my billing role to shrink, though the longer period lets me test customer explanation work while earning. I cannot assume that work survives full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use one approved afternoon a month to sit with the support team and write a plain explanation for a corrected bill. I’d take the free utility-rules course at home one evening a week. In the first year after 2031, if code work ends, I’d apply only for real customer-support openings that pay enough for our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I have more time to practise than in the two-year picture. I would not spend the five-month buffer on a course with no job attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the explanation skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a support colleague to mark my explanation of the power-reset bill. If a customer could not understand it, I need another try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the approved afternoon is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my manager refuses the afternoon, I’d use the free rules course and ask support for feedback after work. I would not pay tuition until an actual vacancy asks for it and the family can afford it.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to test billing explanations.
I know **2034 robots** follow the change in code and school planning.
think: I expect **billing code** work to shrink despite warning.
I cannot assume **customer explanations** remain paid after full thinking AI.
do: **Write** one corrected-bill explanation monthly during approved support time.
**Complete** the free rules course and ask support for feedback after work if approved time is refused.
**Apply** for real mortgage-paying support openings if coding ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about shrinking work, with more time to test a skill.
S3.quote: I would not spend the five-month buffer on a course with no job attached.
fieldNote: She tests **customer explanation** while earning and keeps the free course available if approval fails.
Her **paid-role search** requires actual openings and enough mortgage income.

steps.text: Write monthly bill explanations if support time approved; otherwise study free rules and ask for feedback
Apply for real support jobs paying the mortgage if coding ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to document meter rules properly. Thinking AI reaches code and school planning in 2036; hands-on robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect our wages to hold for the next few years, but I would not call five months of savings permanent safety. AGI by 2036 could make management postpone a useful pay talk today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking odd bills against readings and ask my manager for a written pay-review date this year. I’d keep saving 220 monthly while both incomes hold. In the first year after 2036, if coding ends, I’d search actual local openings and compare their pay before moving the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the future, but my own job and the mortgage look steady for now. I want the current rules written down while the team remembers them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which rule would you document first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the specialist to document the power-reset rule with me this quarter. It helps the next worker and shows my manager what the team actually knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the children for another role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila and I would keep the children at their present school unless a real job offer pays enough for a move. We would not change their routine for a prediction.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to document meter rules.
I know **2039 robots** follow the earlier code and school-planning shift.
think: I expect **household wages** to hold for the next few years.
I would still ask for **current pay** to be reviewed before distant AI changes.
do: **Keep** checking bills, document rules and request a written pay-review date this year.
**Search** real local openings after 2036 if coding ends.
feel: **Uneasy** about future work, with current bills manageable.
S4.quote: AGI by 2036 could make management postpone a useful pay talk today.
fieldNote: Her **five-month cushion** and two present wages permit a measured decade-long plan.
She still requests a **pay-review date** now and will move children only for a real affordable offer.

steps.text: Keep checking meter bills and documenting power-reset rules

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my code and Leila’s school planning could change together. Written severance, paid time to learn billing explanations and income help we qualify for would help. Five months is a buffer, not a promise of another job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who explains a wrong energy bill to a parent choosing between heat and groceries. A correct-looking energy bill can still carry a wrong charge.

headlineQuote: A correct-looking energy bill can still carry a wrong charge.
portrait: Wendy is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree and average skill in energy billing code.
She has **never used AI** and traces meter readings line by line before approving a customer charge.
Her partner’s **school planning** faces thinking AI alongside her code; five months saved cushions but cannot replace two wages.
She tests **approved tools cautiously**, uses free or approved learning and seeks actual jobs that cover the mortgage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut both billing-code and school-planning income before the family adjusts.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid learning time and eligible income help would support the family.
